resolutions: A nonactive Result is derived from a typed imperfective active Source; a copied target string or documentary example cannot authorize it.
The six visible suffix families are realizations of the three nonactive cores o, lo, and hua, not six unrelated grammatical controls.
Written oa and loa cannot erase the grammatical o-hua and lo-hua boundaries.
A single licensed nonactive Result is selected automatically; the user chooses only when the owner issues two or more valid Results.
The perfective nonactive stem depends on the imperfective nonactive stem and is not a separately typed answer.
Regular lō uses the typed active imperfective base already available to the grammar and does not require a future-base control.
Final ya is removed only under the typed Class B root-plus-ya analysis; visible hyphenation is evidence but never authority.
Vowel quantity is preserved during boundary-insensitive lexical identity matching and cannot be silently folded away.
Class C final i plus ā and o plus ā behavior is derived from the typed final-shape and quantity frames.
Class D final long ā receives its reduced written realization before lō automatically and never exposes a macron switch.
Licensed exceptional long-vowel behavior comes from the owner-issued active identity or lexical formation license, not from user-supplied output.
The ca-h, ya-uh, and huāl-la-uh lo-hua Results use their owner-issued suppletive bases rather than a general spelling rewrite.
In hui-tz, itqui-tz, and huica-tz, the typed formation record identifies the compound member that receives lo-hua.
The huica-tz lo-hua and o-hua Results remain distinct valid alternatives and neither is silently preferred.
Clickable cues explain the selected source-to-result operation but never authorize or reconstruct the nonactive Result from display text.
The ō formation is licensed by the typed final environment and is not a suffix option offered to every Source.
Final-vowel deletion before ō is automatic and creates a replacive imperfective base rather than importing the active perfective stem.
The s-to-x and qu-to-c results follow the typed source-final shape and are not exposed as sound-change switches.
A listed lō alternative beside ō remains a real Result choice; the application supplies no silent default.
The narrow transitive ta and postvocalic ti routes and the licensed intransitive ō routes remain typed exceptions rather than productive guesses.
The o-hua formation keeps the o and hua units grammatically separate even when a traditional written projection joins them.
Final-vowel deletion before o-hua is derived from the active Source and cannot be supplied as a user-authored base.
Deletion of remaining final w and compensatory lengthening of o are one owner-issued operation, not two choices.
The o-hua consonant changes are derived from the typed source-final shape and cannot be authorized by an English gloss or copied example.
A final-ni o-hua Result is offered only beside the other licensed nonactive Result and never becomes a general optional switch.
Rare transitive o-hua sources require their typed lexical license; transitivity alone cannot manufacture the formation.
The hua formation is licensed from typed i- and o-final Sources and does not arise from a written final a.
Long ī and ō are preserved before hua, while short final i normally lengthens automatically.
Traditional a after o is a written projection that cannot hide or replace the grammatical hua suffix.
The narrow ci-to-xī replacement and other lexical exceptions remain owner-issued facts rather than manual repair controls.
Transitive and Class C hua extensions occur only for licensed Sources and cannot be inferred from final letters alone.
When hua competes with o-hua, lō, or hua-lō, the user selects the intended final Result; vowel behavior and boundary structure remain derived.
A determinate ō, o-hua, or hua Result proceeds immediately through the familiar voice workflow without displaying an unnecessary formation control.
Hua-lō is issued only for the listed Sources as a free variant of hua and cannot be generalized from rarity or spelling.
The user chooses hua or hua-lō only when both complete Results are licensed; frequency never supplies a default.
Every authorized nonactive Result belongs to Class A regardless of the active Source class, and no class control is shown after derivation.
The A-1 and A-2 implementation profiles preserve Class A boundary behavior without turning the profile name into a user choice.
The nonactive perfective stem is derived from its imperfective nonactive counterpart and cannot be typed or selected independently.
Final o quantity in lō, ō, and hua-lō is determined by the following typed morphs, not by a vowel-length switch.
The same nonactive record can therefore expose long and reduced imperfective or perfective realizations without multiplying grammatical Results.
Ordinary mood, tense, and VNC selection consumes the Class A nonactive stem; no separate Lesson 20 exception control remains.
